questions.q: What were the only two things Mr. Herriot gave Tricki during the first two days of his stay at the surgery?
questions.a: Correct answer: Water and a warm bed. A wrong answer (e.g., "medicine," "special diet," "eggs and wine") reveals the student has confused Mrs. Pumphrey's later offerings with Herriot's actual treatment, showing they haven't distinguished between the owner's misguided care and the vet's scientific method.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Tricki did not eat for the first two days and how this was part of the cure.
questions.a: Correct answer: Tricki refused food because his system was overloaded from constant overfeeding; the fasting allowed his digestive system to rest and reset. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was sad," "he missed Mrs. Pumphrey") reveals the student is projecting human emotions onto the dog instead of understanding the physiological rationale Herriot employs.

questions.q: The text says Tricki "joined the gang" and was "jostled," "rolled over," and "hunted rats." Using these details, write a 40-word answer explaining how the other dogs contributed to his recovery.
questions.a: Correct answer: The pack forced Tricki into physical activity — running, wrestling, hunting — which built muscle, burned fat, and taught him normal canine behaviour. A wrong answer that only mentions "he played with them" misses the *compulsory* nature of the exercise and the specific verbs that show intensity, costing marks for lack of textual precision.

questions.q: Compare Tricki's condition when he arrived ("bloated sausage," "bloodshot eyes," "listless") with his condition at departure ("transformed," "hard muscles," "spring in his step"). What does this contrast reveal about the story's view on pet care?
questions.a: Correct answer: The contrast shows that indulgent overfeeding harms animals while disciplined, natural living restores health; the story privileges veterinary science over sentimental pampering. A wrong answer that merely lists the physical changes without linking them to the *ideological* conflict (science vs. sentiment) fails to meet the "analyze" demand of board questions.

questions.q: Mrs. Pumphrey calls the recovery "a triumph of surgery." Evaluate the irony in this statement: was it truly a surgical triumph? Justify your view with evidence.
questions.a: Correct answer: No — it is verbal irony. No surgery occurred; the "triumph" was simple husbandry (fasting, exercise, pack life). Herriot allows the phrase to spare her feelings and underscore that the *real* cure was non-medical. A wrong answer that takes the phrase literally ("yes, the surgery worked") misses the central ironic device and the author's critique of anthropomorphic pet care.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Tricki's perspective on the third day at the surgery, showing his physical sensations and attitude toward the other dogs.
questions.a: A strong entry uses sensory details (hunger pangs, sore muscles, smell of rats), shows reluctance turning into engagement, and reflects the "underdog" status among the pack. A poor entry writes Tricki as a human child missing his "mummy" or uses no textual verbs ("jostled," "hunted"), revealing failure to adopt the canine perspective the text establishes.
